methodological_rigor.justification: Large statewide retrospective cohort (n=12,096 for KM; n=7,191 complete-case for multivariable Cox) in Espirito Santo, Brazil, using deterministic linkage between the Hospital Cancer Registry (SIS-RHC) and state Mortality Information System (SIM) covering 2000-2016 with follow-up to 2021. Strengths: registry-based population-level coverage, cause-specific Cox modeling addressing competing risks, explicit testing of proportional hazards assumption with appropriate exclusion of violators, STROBE-declared reporting. Limitations acknowledged: no comorbidity/income/insurance data (residual confounding), no treatment timing data (immortal-time bias), complete-case analysis with substantial missingness in some variables (family history 50.87%, disease status 53.04%, reason for no treatment 83.01%), staging missing 25.13%. Statistical methods are appropriate and well-justified.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Individual large retrospective cohort (Oxford 2b). Clinically and epidemiologically relevant for cancer-control policy in Brazil: identifies stage at diagnosis and public-vs-private referral pathway as key determinants of breast-cancer-specific survival, directly informing health-service planning. The 17-fold mortality hazard for stage IV vs. stage I and 17% reduced mortality for private-sector referral are policy-relevant findings for a middle-income oncology network.

reporting_quality.justification: STROBE is explicitly cited and largely followed: study design, setting, participants, variables, outcome definitions, statistical methods, proportional-hazards testing, and a dedicated strengths/limitations section. 95% CIs and p-values are reported for key estimates. Gaps include no participant flow diagram in the provided text, absence of a sensitivity analysis for missing data (only complete-case reported), and no explicit data-sharing statement. Registry data are government-held and likely not publicly reshareable, limiting data availability to 2.

novelty_literature.justification: The finding that stage at diagnosis and private-vs-public referral are associated with breast cancer survival is well-established globally and in Brazil (authors cite several prior Brazilian cohorts including Ferreira et al. with similar 5-year public vs private survival gaps). The novelty lies in (i) the statewide scope of Espirito Santo with HCR-SIM deterministic linkage, which is the first such linkage-based analysis for breast cancer in this state; and (ii) the use of cause-specific Cox modeling in this context. This is a meaningful extension rather than a conceptual advance.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well structured with clear sections, explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria, transparent handling of PH-assumption violations, and a balanced discussion of strengths and limitations. Tables and figures are referenced systematically. The Inclusion/Exclusion criteria appear duplicated in the normalized text (likely a formatting artifact of the conversion). Some sentences are long, but overall prose is clear and appropriate for a public-health oncology audience.

key_strengths: Large statewide cohort (n=12,096) with deterministic HCR-SIM linkage enabling accurate cause-specific mortality ascertainment
Cause-specific Cox modeling with proportional-hazards testing and appropriate exclusion of PH-violating variables
Clear quantification of referral-pathway disparity (private vs SUS HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.75-0.93) after adjustment for stage, metastasis, age, education, year
Explicit STROBE adherence and thoughtful discussion of residual confounding and immortal-time bias
Policy-relevant findings for middle-income oncology care network organization
key_concerns: Substantial missingness for several variables (stage 25.1%, family history 50.9%, treatment status 53.0%, reason for non-treatment 83.0%) with complete-case only (no multiple imputation sensitivity analysis)
No data on comorbidities, income, or insurance, limiting adjustment for known confounders of the public-private gradient
Treatment variables recorded without timing, precluding time-dependent modeling and introducing potential immortal-time bias
Novelty is incremental relative to prior Brazilian survival cohorts
chief_reviewer.rationale: A methodologically solid, appropriately scoped registry-linked statewide cohort with clear limitations; fits a mid-tier specialty or public-health oncology journal after minor revisions (e.g., imputation sensitivity analysis, flow diagram).
